articles.body:
Duas apostas simples de Santa Catarina acertaram cinco números no concurso 3076 de Mega-Sena. O sorteio foi feito na noite desta terça-feira (27).

Ninguém acertou as seis dezenas. O prêmio era de R$ 309,9 milhões e acumulou para R$ 320 milhões.

Veja os números sorteados: 06 - 30 - 32 - 38 - 49 - 57

As duas apostas catarinenses que acertaram cinco números foram feitas de forma digital. Cada uma ganhou R$ 58.086,17 .

Os apostadores são de Itajaí , no Litoral Norte, e Xanxerê , no Oeste.

A probabilidade de vencer em cada concurso varia de acordo com o número de dezenas jogadas e o tipo de aposta realizada. Para um jogo simples, com apenas seis dezenas, que custa R$ 6, a probabilidade de ganhar o prêmio milionário é de 1 em 50.063.860, segundo a Caixa.

Já para uma aposta com 20 dezenas (limite máximo), com o preço de R$ 232.560,00, a probabilidade de acertar o prêmio é de 1 em 1.292, ainda de acordo com a instituição.

articles.title: Família grande? Veja por que o BYD Atto 8 é a escolha mais inteligente e completa | G1
articles.standfirst: Com segurança e conforto para todos, SUV super híbrido tem performance surpreendente para um modelo de sete lugares.
articles.summary: Com segurança e conforto para todos, SUV super híbrido tem performance surpreendente para um modelo de sete lugares.
articles.body:
Com mais de 5m de comprimento, SUV tem espaço impressionante — Foto: Divulgação

Quando a BYD chegou ao Brasil, era comum associar a marca apenas aos modelos 100% elétricos. Hoje, a greentech tem presença consolidada no segmento dos super híbridos com um portfólio diversificado. O BYD Atto 8 é um exemplo: primeiro SUV com mais de cinco metros de comprimento, o modelo premium é a indicação para famílias grandes.

Ter sete lugares já diz muito sobre a proposta, mas o veículo vai além da capacidade de ocupantes. Ao mesmo tempo em que oferece segurança e conforto para todos, o BYD Atto 8 entrega uma performance surpreendente para um SUV desse porte.

A explicação está na nova plataforma Dm-P (Dual Mode Performance): com um motor elétrico em cada eixo, motor 1.5 turbo e tração integral inteligente, o SUV tem 488 cv de potência combinada e vai de 0 a 100 km/h em 4,9 segundos.

Para quem busca um carro com eficiência elétrica no dia a dia e também quer a praticidade do abastecimento, o BYD Atto 8 é a escolha mais inteligente e completa. A autonomia total é de até 900 km, permitindo longas viagens com a família toda.

articles.title: Em eleição acirrada, Israel vai às urnas pela primeira vez desde os ataques do Hamas há 3 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Boca de urna não aponta maioria nem do primeiro-ministro Benjamin Netanyahu, nem da oposição.
articles.summary: Boca de urna não aponta maioria nem do primeiro-ministro Benjamin Netanyahu, nem da oposição.
articles.body:
Israel fez, nesta terça-feira (27), as primeiras eleições desde os atentados terroristas que mataram 1,2 mil pessoas três anos atrás. As pesquisas de boca de urna não indicam que nem o primeiro-ministro Benjamin Netanyahu nem a oposição vão conseguir formar maioria.

O governo de Benjamin Netanyahu foi posto à prova nas urnas. É a primeira votação depois dos atentados terroristas de 7 de outubro de 2023, que desencadearam a guerra na Faixa de Gaza . Logo cedo, parentes das vítimas do maior massacre contra judeus desde o Holocausto pediram uma investigação sobre as falhas que permitiram o ataque.

O voto em Israel não é obrigatório. O eleitor não vota em um candidato, mas sim em uma lista de um partido ou coligação. O parlamento de Israel - o Knesset - fica em Jerusalém. São 120 cadeiras em disputa e um cenário muito dividido: nunca um partido conquistou sozinho a maioria absoluta das vagas. E, por isso, a formação de um governo depende das coalizões. É uma negociação tão acirrada, que até os partidos menores, que conseguem ultrapassar a cláusula de barreira, podem ser decisivos na escolha do novo governo.

Em eleição acirrada, Israel vai às urnas pela primeira vez desde os ataques do Hamas há 3 anos — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Benjamin Netanyahu é o líder do Likud e tenta o sétimo mandato como primeiro-ministro. Em 2022, ele fechou acordos com partidos ultraortodoxos e de extrema-direita para conseguir governar. Uma família votou pela continuidade. A Agam disse que Netanyahu é o único que pode enfrentar os inimigos externos de Israel e destacou a aliança com o presidente americano, Donald Trump.

O principal adversário de Netanyahu é Gadi Eisenkot, ex-chefe das Forças Armadas de Israel, que perdeu um filho e dois sobrinhos na guerra de Gaza e é visto como um homem do povo. Um eleitor disse que Eisenkot é completamente diferente de Netanyahu: " Eu acredito nele. Ele é o homem que vai mudar o governo ".

Vários temas sacodem a disputa, como o aumento do custo de vida; a independência do Poder Judiciário; a isenção dos judeus ortodoxos do alistamento militar; e, principalmente, a forma como os candidatos vão lidar com a segurança em meio aos confrontos históricos com o Irã e os grupos extremistas financiados pelo regime iraniano.

“As eleições israelenses, agora de 2026, elas representam as eleições mais importantes, pelo menos, das últimas décadas no país. Porque ela contrapõe o governo atual, cuja continuidade significaria uma perpetuação da situação bélica e de crise por mais alguns anos ou, talvez, a médio ou longo prazo, por muito mais tempo, contra uma possibilidade de tentativa de sair dessa situação, de resolver essas questões que foram inauguradas no 7 de outubro e de partir para um conserto dos problemas. É essa expressão que eles usam”, diz João Miragaya, mestre em História pela Universidade de Tel Aviv.

articles.title: Parlamentares da Argentina pedem investigação sobre possível fuga de Flávio pelo país, diz jornal  | G1
articles.standfirst: Deputados e senadores querem que governo Milei esclareça se senador brasileiro cruzou a fronteira antes de viajar para os EUA; governo afirma que não há registro de entrada
articles.summary: Deputados e senadores querem que governo Milei esclareça se senador brasileiro cruzou a fronteira antes de viajar para os EUA; governo afirma que não há registro de entrada
articles.body:
Parlamentares de oposição da Argentina cobraram nesta terça-feira (27) uma investigação sobre a possível passagem do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) pelo país antes de sua suposta fuga para os Estados Unidos . O pedido foi feito após um jornal do país indicar que o senador teria passado por Puerto Iguazú, cidade argentina na fronteira com o Brasil.

O governo do presidente Javier Milei , aliado político de Flávio, afirmou que não há registros da entrada do senador no território argentino . A oposição, porém, exige esclarecimentos sobre a possível travessia da fronteira e sobre as circunstâncias da viagem, segundo o jornal espanhol "El País".

O senador estava proibido de deixar o Brasil por uma determinação e do ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Alexandre de Moraes, no âmbito das investigação sobre o financiamento do filme Dark Horse e as suspeitas de lavagem de dinheiro junto do advogado Willer Tomaz.

Flávio deveria ter entregue seus passaportes nesta terça-feira (27), mas não o fez .

A senadora peronista Juliana Di Tullio pediu que o governo argentino esclareça se Flávio usou o território do país para deixar o Brasil.

“O governo argentino, por meio de Diego Santilli [ministro do Interior], deve explicar se Bolsonaro usou nossa fronteira e nosso território para fugir do Brasil”, afirmou.

A deputada Myriam Bregman, da Frente de Esquerda, também cobrou esclarecimentos das autoridades e criticou o discurso de combate ao crime adotado por políticos de direita.

Já o deputado socialista Esteban Paulón apresentou um pedido formal de informações ao Executivo na Câmara dos Deputados argentina. Ele quer saber se existem registros de entrada ou saída de Bolsonaro do país e se o governo recebeu notificações sobre restrições judiciais ou retenção de documentos de viagem.

Entre as hipóteses discutidas pelos congressistas argentinos estão a de que ele teria cruzado a fronteira a pé, com um documento brasileiro, ou utilizado o passaporte italiano.

A Direção Nacional de Migrações da Argentina afirmou que não possui registros da entrada de Flávio Bolsonaro no país. O órgão também informou que verificou a documentação de uma aeronave e de sua tripulação que estavam em Puerto Iguazú. Segundo o governo, os documentos estavam regulares e não havia plano de voo que incluísse a família Bolsonaro.

O porta-voz da Presidência argentina, Adrián Ravier, também declarou que não havia pedido de asilo apresentado por Bolsonaro.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro chega aos EUA, diz BBC | G1
articles.standfirst: Governo Trump informou que concederá vistos ao senador e sua família. No domingo (25), decisão do ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF, proibiu Flávio de deixar o território brasileiro.
articles.summary: Governo Trump informou que concederá vistos ao senador e sua família. No domingo (25), decisão do ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF, proibiu Flávio de deixar o território brasileiro.
articles.body:
O senador Flávio Bolsonaro chegou aos Estados Unidos nesta terça-feira (27), segundo a rede britânica BBC. O veículo afirma, com base em fontes ouvidas sob condição de anonimato, que o candidato derrotado aterrisou no estado da Flórida.

Flávio já se encontrou com o irmão , Eduardo Bolsonaro , que vive no país desde fevereiro de 2025. Antes da votação do último domingo (25), Eduardo aconselhou o irmão a fugir do Brasil caso perdesse as eleições .

Ainda não há informações claras sobre o trajeto usado pelo senador para deixar o Brasil nem se ele pretende morar nos Estados Unidos.

O Departamento de Estado dos EUA deve conceder vistos a Flávio Bolsonaro e a sua família e permitirá a entrada deles no país, segundo informou uma autoridade do órgão à repórter da TV Globo Raquel Krähenbühl.

Mais cedo, a agência de notícias Reuters e o jornal "The New York Times" haviam informado, citando fontes anônimas, que o senador deixou o Brasil rumo aos Estados Unidos. O caso é investigado pela Polícia Federal (PF).

Nas primeiras horas da manhã desta terça, um jornal argentino divulgou que o senador teria saído do Brasil pela fronteira com Puerto Iguazú , na Argentina. Segundo a reportagem do Infobae, Flávio teria cruzado a fronteira para a Argentina usando seu documento de identidade.

"De Puerto Iguazú, viajaria aos Estados Unidos a bordo de um avião Gulfstream G400, de matrícula LV-JQW, pertencente à empresa Baires Fly S.A", informa o site.

Segundo o site de monitoramento aéreo FlightRadar24, a aeronave voou de Buenos Aires para Puerto Iguazú e chegou à cidade às 23h45, no horário de Brasília. O avião, no entanto, não havia deixado a cidade desde então, segundo os registros.

Não há confirmação até o momento se Flávio chegou a estar na aeronave e se teria trocado de avião para seguir para os Estados Unidos.

O candidato à presidência do Brasil, Flávio Bolsonaro, do Partido Liberal (PL), discursa após perder o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, em Brasília, Brasil, em 25 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Agustin Marcarian

Na manhã desta terça, o controle de imigração do governo argentino afirmou que não havia registro de entrada de Flávio Bolsonaro no país .

A informação corrobora com informações da Polícia Federal, reveladas pelo blog da Andréia Sadi. Segundo o órgão, não há registro de passagem de Flávio por nenhum ponto regular de controle migratório brasileiro .

Na noite de domingo (25), o ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), determinou que Flávio Bolsonaro entregasse seus passaportes. O senador, no entanto, descumpriu a ordem e não entregou o passaporte à PF no prazo determinado, até as 11h desta terça-feira (27).

A decisão foi dada em processo em que Flávio e o advogado Willer Tomaz são investigados por lavagem de dinheiro, em um suposto esquema que envolveria empresas de Tomaz e bets. Os dois confirmam que são amigos, mas negam que sejam sócios e qualquer irregularidade.

Flávio Bolsonaro também é formalmente investigado pela Polícia Federal (PF) em inquérito aberto para apurar a possível prática de crimes relacionados ao financiamento da produção do filme "Dark Horse", sobre a trajetória do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro.

articles.summary: A historic London house on a street believed to have inspired Harry Potter’s Diagon Alley has gone on the market for £1.595 million.
articles.body: A historic London house on a street believed to have inspired Harry Potter’s Diagon Alley has gone on the market for £1.595 million. The two-bedroom property, located on Goodwin’s Court in Covent Garden, dates back to around 1700 and is said to have inspired the magical shopping street from the popular wizarding franchise.The property, which has retained several of its original features, is also believed to have inspired Ollivanders wand shop and the darker Knockturn Alley. However, these connections remain unconfirmed.Harry Potter-inspired house gets £405,000 price cutThe house, which originally went on the market for £2 million, was withdrawn before being relisted last month for £1.595 million. According to the Unique Property Company, the property has attracted considerable interest since being relisted, particularly from buyers in the US.Built shortly after the Great Fire of London, the historic home sits on a narrow, cobbled passage that has become a popular destination for Harry Potter fans, often referred to as Potterheads. The street is visited by themed walking tours every day, with its old-world charm adding to its association with the wizarding world.One of the features that adds to the atmosphere is a gas lamp above the steps leading to the house’s black front door.In its listing, the estate agency described the property as “a rare survivor of a building type reflecting the conditions of London’s Georgian working-classes and a living piece of London’s rich history”. It also highlighted the house’s more recent association with Ollivanders Wand Shop in the Harry Potter film franchise.Historic house features stone steps that could date back to medieval timesThe property, which originally served as a haberdashery, has several distinctive features that reflect its long history. Four worn stone steps sit beneath the front door, and their condition has led to speculation that they may have been reused from an older building.According to the property listing, the wear on the steps is unlikely to have resulted solely from customers visiting the former shop. They may have been salvaged from an ancient building demolished around the time Goodwin’s Court was constructed, potentially dating them to the medieval period or even earlier. Their exact origins, however, remain uncertain.Simon Stone, managing partner at the Unique Property Company, said the house was a rare find in London.“Number 1 Goodwin’s Court is such a rare find in London these days,” he said, according to SWNS.“It’s a home that’s been conserved rather than have the history erased. It’s so atmospheric.”Stone added that the property offers a sense of stepping back in time, despite being just moments away from the bustle of central London.“It’s a property that takes you to another time entirely and it’s so quiet, you forget that just five seconds away, you’re in the thick of one of the world’s busiest capital cities,” he said.Original Georgian features survive inside the £1.6 million homeInside, the house retains several period details, including an intricate bow window on the raised ground-floor reception room. Dating back to the early 18th century, the window remains largely in its original state.The kitchen connects to a Georgian-style tiled shower room with an antique toilet and washbasin. The space occupies an area associated with the former “Night Soil Alley”, a passage used for transporting human waste in earlier times.The property also offers a glimpse into its former life as a shop. Two softly worn patches on the floorboards are believed to mark where a shopkeeper once stood.With its historic architecture, unusual period details and reported connection to the Harry Potter films, the house offers a distinctive piece of London history for buyers willing to pay £1.595 million.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Ex-Met officer who served in Couzens unit found guilty of rape
articles.summary: Mark Tyrrell is also convicted of sexual assault and trying to delete messages he sent the woman.
articles.body:
A former Metropolitan Police officer who served in the same command as Wayne Couzens has been found guilty of raping a woman.

Mark Tyrrell, 57, was convicted at Southwark Crown Court of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice by trying to delete messages he had sent her.

Jurors heard he had sex with the woman, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, after she repeatedly said no, then asked her: "Do you realise that what I've just done, that was rape?"

He was cleared of a further count of rape, four of assault by penetration and eight of sexual assault.

Tyrrell, of Meltham, West Yorkshire, had been attached to the Met's Parliamentary and Diplomatic Protection Command, the unit in which Couzens and David Carrick, both convicted rapists, also served.

Prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC said that when the woman resisted his advances "he simply chose to take what he wanted". Concerns were first raised when officers visiting her home on an unrelated matter found him hiding beside her bed.

In one message, he apologised for "being a sex offender" and "for ruining your life by being in it".

Ex-Met Police officer trained to support rape victims accused of rape

Giving evidence, Tyrrell said sex between them had always been consensual and "there was never any forcefulness to it".

He had already admitted misconduct in a public office and a separate count of perverting the course of justice, for persuading the woman to lie to police about why he was in her bedroom.

Ch Supt Sara Leach said: "This kind of conduct is abhorrent but even more so when it is carried out by a serving officer, who had gained the trust of the victim.

"We remain appalled that someone like this was serving within our organisation and it is right he has been brought to justice."

Sarah Everard, 33, was kidnapped, raped and murdered by Couzens in March 2021. He is serving a whole-life order.

Carrick, a former armed officer, is serving 36 life sentences for attacks on more than a dozen women.

Tyrrell resigned from the force in September 2023 after being arrested and suspended.

He will be sentenced at the same court on 16 December.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Dubbing the Election Commission’s affidavit in Supreme Court as “deceptive, deceitful and duplicitous”, Congress Tuesday said CEC Gyanesh Kumar
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Dubbing the Election Commission’s affidavit in Supreme Court as “deceptive, deceitful and duplicitous”, Congress Tuesday said CEC Gyanesh Kumar has been taking unilateral decisions and the EC’s claims on Form 6 are contradictory.Taking to X, Congress spokesperson Jairam Ramesh wrote, “Oh what a tangled web we weave, when first we practice to deceive.” He said that as per the EC’s claims, major SIR orders were formally approved by all three ECs.“But two election commissioners objected on record to grave violations and illegal actions taking place on orders of CEC — their objections were disregarded. The commissioners were not even informed and learnt of these decisions from the news. This is not unanimity but unilateral decision-making,” he said.Ramesh said EC’s stand on “illegal amendment to Form 6” is deceptive as it first claimed SC had approved the new declaration attached to Form 6 but changed its tune after SC contradicted its claim. “It now claims the new declaration form is separate, and Form 6 was not amended. articles.title: Two Massachusetts cranberry bogs were too unprofitable to farm, until owners installed solar fields 10 feet above the vines; income from solar land leases helped restore berry production without abandoning agriculture
articles.summary: Two cranberry bogs in Massachusetts that had stopped making money have returned to active farming after solar panels were installed ten feet above the
articles.body: Two cranberry bogs in Massachusetts that had stopped making money have returned to active farming after solar panels were installed ten feet above the crops. According to reporting by Electrek, the project uses a method called agrivoltaics, which allows farmers to grow crops and generate solar power on the same land. The arrangement gives farmers a steady income from leasing their land for solar energy without having to sell it or stop growing cranberries. This guaranteed income helped cover high running costs, improve soil health, and restart berry harvests that had become too costly for years. The approach combines farming with solar power generation. It also addresses concerns among farming communities that solar projects take up valuable farmland and reduce food production.Dual land use restores historic bogsGrowing cranberries in Massachusetts requires major spending on pest control, irrigation, sanding, and harvesting equipment. In recent years, falling crop prices and rising costs have forced several family-owned farms across New England to leave their bogs unused or consider selling their land to property developers. The two Massachusetts sites chosen for the agrivoltaics project had stopped commercial farming because the cost of maintaining the bogs was higher than the market value of the cranberries they produced. To bring the land back into use, developers built steel support structures that raised the solar panels ten feet above the bogs. This height allows traditional farming equipment, including tractors, harvesters, and irrigation systems, to work underneath the panels without getting in the way. The design also leaves wide gaps between rows of panels so enough sunlight can reach the cranberry vines below. Early farming assessments found that the partial shade helped keep soil temperatures lower during heatwaves, reduced water loss through evaporation, and protected the delicate vines from too much heat.Financial stability through solar leasingThe financial model depends on long-term land lease agreements between farm owners and solar energy developers. Under these agreements, solar developers pay landowners fixed annual fees for the right to produce electricity and send it to the local power grid. As reported by Electrek, this predictable income helps farmers manage changes in cranberry prices. The lease payments provided the money needed to restore the unused bogs. Farmers removed weeds, repaired irrigation channels, and planted new cranberry vines beneath the solar panels. By earning money from both solar leases and cranberry sales, the farms created two sources of income. This approach also helps protect farmland from being sold for industrial or residential development.State policy supports agricultural solarThe success of these cranberry bogs fits with wider state programmes that encourage solar power projects on working farmland. Massachusetts created specific incentives through its Solar Massachusetts Renewable Target (SMART) programme to support agrivoltaic projects. The scheme offers extra payments for each kilowatt-hour of electricity produced by solar arrays that allow farming to continue underneath. It also sets strict rules for panel height and the amount of light that must reach crops, helping ensure that agricultural production can continue. University researchers, including teams from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, have been studying crop yields, soil moisture, and light levels at elevated solar test sites across the region. Their ongoing research looks at how different crops respond to partial shade and how changing the angle of solar panels can balance electricity production with farming needs. Data collected from working farms in Plymouth and Barnstable counties shows that some cranberry varieties maintain steady yields under partial shade. The findings also indicate that irrigation needs can fall because less water evaporates from the ground.Expanding agrivoltaics across New EnglandCombining solar panels with cranberry bogs reflects a wider trend across the northeastern United States. High land prices and limited capacity in electricity networks have increased competition between renewable energy developers and farmers for available land. Agrivoltaic systems are also being tested on other types of farmland in the region, including livestock pastures, vegetable fields, and berry farms. Generating electricity for local power networks while continuing to grow food allows rural communities to meet clean energy targets without reducing local food production. For Massachusetts' cranberry industry, one of the oldest commercial farming industries in the United States, elevated solar panels offer a practical way to preserve historic farmland while producing clean electricity for nearby communities.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Sydney couple turned a 1907 tram substation in Rozelle into a four-bedroom family home, and the historic former transport building sold at auction for $3.9 million
articles.summary: A 1907 tram substation in Rozelle, converted into a four-bedroom family home, sold at auction in Sydney in August 2023 above its $3.7 million price guide.
articles.body: A 1907 tram substation in Rozelle, converted into a four-bedroom family home, sold at auction in Sydney in August 2023 above its $3.7 million price guide. The heritage building at 10 Hancock Street is the last intact structure of its kind in New South Wales, and it still carries the industrial character of its working past inside a 470-square-metre interior. Its owners, a Sydney couple, adapted the former warehouse office space into a family home while carefully keeping the raw architecture that defines the building. The sale put a rare piece of Sydney’s inner west transport history into new hands.How a tram substation that powered Sydney’s inner west until 1958 ended up as a homeThe building at 10 Hancock Street was the Balmain tram substation. It dates to 1907 and supplied power to trams throughout the inner west until it was decommissioned in 1958, as buses took over Sydney’s streets.Simon Duffy, executive director of Taronga Zoo, and his husband Walter Murphy, head of service excellence in Westpac’s customer solutions division, spotted it on a neighbourhood walk in 2020. Duffy told Domain that life is short and they felt they had to take the opportunity. He said they were struck by the building’s sense of history and its “raw beauty”.A turbine door, lettered metal beams and a rolling crane remain from the building’s pastDespite the conversion, the rustic bones of the substation remain. A huge door once allowed turbines to be moved in and out, and massive metal beams still carry their original lettering. An almost sculptural industrial crane sits at the centre of the building, hung with pulleys and chains.Duffy also said the original horizontal crane is one of the home’s most striking features. It could roll along the length of the building and was used to move circuits around.Mezzanine bedrooms and a double-height living room turn an industrial shell into a homeMezzanine bedrooms leave room for a vast, double-height living room. Duffy said visitors were blown away by the scale, especially when they stepped through the front door and looked up.The couple divided the space into zones, partly with furniture, including a 16-seat dining table inherited from the previous owners. Their changes to the building were mostly minor, Duffy said: a better bathroom, an improved kitchen and a more workable layout. The main task was deciding which parts needed to feel cosier and where open space worked best, since the building already had good bones.Treetop windows, a native garden next door and a ground-floor retreat suit family lifeHuge windows look out over the treetops, offer glimpses of the city and flood the rooms with natural light, which kept the couple’s collection of indoor plants happy. From their mezzanine bedroom, Duffy said he woke to birdsong from the native garden next door. Neighbours planted it, and they own the converted stable that once housed the horse-drawn carts that serviced the tram line. He told the same publication that the room felt light and bright but also cosy.The sons’ bedrooms and the guest bedroom are more private and less open, though equally roomy. The children also had a ground-floor retreat suited to video games and movie nights with friends.Why the owners were selling a home they loved and the local rituals they wanted to keepWith their eldest son heading to university, Duffy said the huge space had become too big for the three remaining family members. They were also spending a growing number of weekends at their beach house on the South Coast.The couple had lived in Rozelle and its surroundings for almost all of their 24 years together, and they wanted to downsize nearby. They hoped to keep their routines of bay walks with their two dogs, Saturday mornings at the local organic growers’ market and drinks at one of the area’s many small bars. Duffy said they were just 20 steps from a coffee shop they loved, close to a French bakery and surrounded by grocers. He added that they hoped to find the same in their next property, along with good neighbours.The auction on 7 August 2023 ended at $3.9 million for the converted tram substationThe property went to auction on 7 August 2023 and sold for $3.9 million, according to Domain’s sold listing. The listing, handled by BresicWhitney Inner West, presented the building as a converted warehouse home inside a historic tramway substation. It said the original character had been carefully preserved and that the space had been turned into a flexible four-bedroom home with separate living areas suited to family life.You use AI every day. articles.title: LAPD union leader warns against mayoral candidate Nithya Raman's stances on public drug use, police staffing
articles.summary: Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman clashed with Graham Stephan on "The Iced Coffee Hour" over public drug use and police staffing as the LAPD union warns against her policies.
articles.body: Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman faced tough questions Sunday over public drug use and police staffing, prompting the city's police union to accuse her of contradicting her previous voting record as she campaigns to unseat Mayor Karen Bass. During an appearance with host Graham Stephan on "The Iced Coffee Hour" podcast, Raman suggested certain calls involving people experiencing homelessness could be handled without armed police officers, arguing that the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) would be unable to intervene if no crime was taking place. "Like the issue that you had with a person who is on your sidewalk, who is clearly homeless, who is maybe not someone you feel comfortable talking to," she said. "LAPD would come out to that situation and not be able to do anything, right? If they're not — if there's not a crime happening there. If they're not a threat to themselves." Stephan challenged her characterization, emphasizing that the individuals he described were openly using illegal drugs. "Well, there is a crime. They're doing drugs," he said. WATCH: LEFT-WING LA MAYOR FACES REALITY TV CHALLENGER’S BLUNT TAKEDOWNS IN HEATED MAYORAL DEBATE The exchange prompted a response from Los Angeles Police Protective League (LAPPL) Vice President Chris Wecker, who questioned Raman's commitment to maintaining police staffing in a statement to Fox News Digital. Wecker pointed to her opposition earlier this year to a proposal intended to offset officer retirements. "No, there are not enough police officers now to keep residents and officers safe," he said. "What has Angelenos scratching their heads is the stark contrast between what Candidate Raman is saying today and what Councilmember Raman voted on earlier this year. This year she voted against hiring 170 officers to replace those who were retiring. This wouldn't have increased the number of officers; it simply would have kept the number of officers the same." "So, who do Angelenos believe: Candidate Raman or Councilmember Raman?" Raman's opposition is documented in her voting record. She was one of four council members who voted against a January proposal authorizing funding for 130 recruits — the final portion of a 170-recruit hiring plan that began in December and brought total expected recruits for the fiscal year to about 410, Fox 11 reported. The measure passed 9-4. LA MAYORAL RACE HEADS TO NOVEMBER RUNOFF AS KAREN BASS FACES MAMDANI-STYLE SOCIALIST Stephan described residents encountering people using drugs in alleys and near homes, including complaints that officers were slow to respond. Raman advocated expanding unarmed crisis response programs to handle certain calls. Wecker rejected the idea that public drug use should be among the situations handled by unarmed responders, warning that the encounters could become dangerous. "We support unarmed responses to some calls for service. Public drug use is not one of those calls," he told Fox News Digital. "These are some of the most dangerous and unpredictable calls to which officers must respond. We can't imagine a methamphetamine or cocaine user paying any attention to a clinician, and we believe the responding clinician would actually escalate the situation, putting them in harm's way and necessitating an armed response." "It sounds good until good people start getting hurt," he continued. KAREN BASS RIPPED AFTER SUGGESTING TAXPAYER-FUNDED DENTAL CARE FOR METH USERS As Stephan repeatedly pressed Raman about whether Los Angeles needed additional police officers, the candidate defended her proposal to prevent further staffing declines while shifting certain responsibilities away from sworn personnel. "I want to maintain the size of our police force. That's what — that's where we're at right now," Raman said. She maintained that hiring civilian employees for administrative work and expanding alternative response teams would allow existing officers to concentrate on criminal activity. She also blamed bureaucratic delays for recruitment difficulties. When Stephan questioned why she considered the current number of officers sufficient, Raman acknowledged that Los Angeles has fewer officers per capita than cities such as New York and Chicago. She advocated studying call volumes and deployment requirements before determining the appropriate staffing level. SEE IT: LA DEM CANDIDATES TORCHED BY DISGUSTED RESIDENTS AFTER ‘DISGRACEFUL’ DEBATE: ‘BOTH BAD’ The debate comes as Bass has pursued additional LAPD hiring. Her 2026-27 budget proposal called for 510 new officer hires. The city subsequently adopted a budget maintaining that hiring target. However, the incumbent mayor has also supported expanding civilian crisis response. In July, Bass announced more than $2 million in federal funding for the city's CIRCLE program, which deploys unarmed mental health professionals to certain nonviolent calls involving people experiencing homelessness or mental health crises. Alex Stack, a spokesperson for Mayor Karen Bass' re-election campaign, said in a statement to Fox News Digital: "Nithya Raman voted against hiring more police officers every chance she got in city council, and we have less officers now directly because of her. Mayor Bass has been working to expand the size of the police force to 9,500 officers in order to reduce 911 response times and make our neighborhoods safer." articles.title: Search continues for married couple Leo and Katherine Lindeman, missing from Missouri home
articles.summary: 73-year-old Leo and 74-year-old Katherine Lindeman have been missing from their Anderson, Missouri, home since Sept. 16. The McDonald County Sheriff’s Office is investigating.
articles.body: You could say that Leo and Katherine Lindeman live off the grid. The couple, both in their 70s, bought 15 acres of land in rural Anderson, Missouri, in 2021. Leo, a retired mason, built the home himself. Solar panels powered their appliances, and without air conditioning, they often left the doors and windows open to ventilate the house. Cell service was poor, so they primarily kept up with family via text. For Leo and Katherine, it was perfect. They had friends in the area, but they spent most of their time on their property. “They really just wanted to retire and have peacefulness,” Leo’s sister-in-law Debra Lindeman told Dateline. But around September 16, 2026, that peaceful life was shattered when Leo, Katherine, and their dog, Itty Bitty, vanished without a trace. Dateline spoke with Debra and her daughter, LaShawnda Lindeman. Both live in Wichita, Kansas, and say the family received a call from Missouri law enforcement on September 24 informing them that a neighbor had reported Leo and Katherine missing. According to LaShawnda, her aunt and uncle had a standing weekly dinner date with their neighbor. On September 15, Katherine went to the dinner while Leo stayed home, waiting for an appointment with an electrician. The next day, September 16, the neighbor stopped by the Lindeman home to return dishes from the night before. He found the doors and windows open, but no sign of Leo or Katherine. He left the dishes on the table with a note. “He called them, texted them. He didn’t hear from them,” LaShawnda said. The following week, when the Lindemans failed to show up for their regular dinner, the neighbor became concerned. “And when it came and went that they were supposed to come and have dinner with him, then he went back out there to check on them,” LaShawnda said. When the neighbor returned, the dishes and note he’d left the previous week were still on the table, and there was no sign of the Lindemans. LaShawnda says the neighbor called the McDonald County Sheriff’s Department to report Leo and Katherine missing on September 24. On September 26, the McDonald County Sheriff’s Office released a missing persons poster for Leo and Katherine on its Facebook page which confirmed they were reported missing on September 24 and gave an approximate date of disappearance as September 16. Dateline reached out to the McDonald County Sheriff’s Office for further information but has not yet received a response. On September 28, LaShawnda and other members of the family traveled from Wichita to the Lindeman property to help with the search. “The gate was left unlocked, the home was left unlocked,” LaShawnda said. The couple’s vehicle was also on the property. “When they left, they left — everything was in place,” Debra said. “The bed was made still. The house was in perfect order.” According to Debra, the couple’s personal belongings, including cellphones, IDs, and Katherine’s purse, were found inside the home. Their medications were also left behind, particularly concerning given that Leo had survived five heart attacks and Katherine was living with lupus. “All the medication was still there,” LaShawnda said. According to the family, none of this was typical behavior for Leo and Katherine. If the couple were traveling for an extended period, they would have closed up the house and taken their essential medications. That same day the family arrived, a private drone operator from Arkansas met up with them at the property to help search for Leo and Katherine. The search turned up nothing. LaShawnda says that on September 29, the McDonald County Sheriff’s Office processed the home and vehicle, and searched the property with canine units. “Nothing has been found,” LaShawnda said. “The dogs didn’t hit on anything.” As the weeks pass, the Lindeman family fears the worst. “If somebody came and took them and kidnapped them, did anybody see them anywhere?” Debra wondered. “I’m sure there’s somebody out there knows something,” LaShawnda said. The Lindeman family is counting on somebody to come forward. “The ultimate goal is to bring our family home,” LaShawnda said. Leo Lindeman is 73 years old, 5’7”, and 145 lbs. Katherine Lindeman is 74 years old, 5’2”, and 150 lbs. Their small, white dog, Itty Bitty, is also missing. Anyone with information regarding Leo and Katherine Lindeman is asked to call the McDonald County Dispatch Center at 417-223-4318. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: Marry Mubaiwa: Ex-wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president freed after collapse of attempted murder case
articles.summary: Marry Mubaiwa had been held on remand for seven years after being charged in 2019 for her then husband's attempted murder.
articles.body:
The former wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president has been freed from remand after seven years while on trial for his attempted murder.

Marry Mubaiwa was charged in 2019, after her then husband Gen Constantino Chiwenga accused her of trying to impede his medical treatment in South Africa.

Ordering her release, a magistrate said Mubaiwa had suffered mental, physical and financial prejudice during the trial, state-owned daily the Herald said.

The ruling was made after the state asked for the trial to be postponed by a month in order to engage witnesses.

Her lawyer described the ruling as a victory that had come too late, because her client's rights had been violated by the delay in the trial.

Speaking outside court in the capital Harare on Tuesday, the lawyer added that if the state moved for a new trial, they would deal with it when it happened.

Mubaiwa was accused of attempting to kill Chiwenga, while he was in hospital in Pretoria. The vice-president then went to China for four months of treatment.

Mubaiwa was remanded in custody and denied bail.

According to the New Zimbabwe news website, Mubaiwa celebrated her release outside court, and said justice had been achieved and that she was proud of her lawyer.

In 2017, Chiwenga played a key role in overthrowing then President Robert Mugabe.

articles.title: SC: Cannot let pharma industry ‘run amok’ in name of free market
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday said the pharma industry cannot be allowed to “run amok” in the name of free market to fix the maximum retail price (MRP)
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday said the pharma industry cannot be allowed to “run amok” in the name of free market to fix the maximum retail price (MRP) of medicines at an exponentially high level, which in some cases happens to be over 1,000% of the price at which they are sold to retailers.Expressing anguish over the suffering of the common man who had to pay the price, a bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said the court is “pained by the loot” and repeatedly asked Centre to explain the rationale behind allowing a high MRP and who ultimately benefits from the policy. It reserved its order on plea to bring all non-patented medicines and medical consumables under price control mechanism like scheduled drugs.Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati, who had to face a volley of questions from the bench, tried to convince the court that govt was aware of the problem and that was why it recently decided to cap the price of anti-cancer drugs. But the court responded that govt “woke up” only after it intervened and passed harsh observations on the prevailing system.She, however, said the deliberation was already on and SC’s intervention expedited it. “People are living in a daydream that someday they will benefit from the drugs prices control order (DPCO)... The policy is only to give benefit to the corporate. We are thinking from the point of view of poor patients,” SC observed. Bhati, thereafter, submitted that medicine prices in India are among the lowest in the world due to free market and govt cannot take control of the entire pharma market, but the bench told her, “You are either not aware about the problem or not keen to solve the problem... Why is the entire system working for the benefit of few people?”“Ordinarily, where there is substantial competition, there is no need to regulate prices. It is not that the govt has left the market unregulated but the complete control of the market is not feasible,” Bhati said, adding that the issue pertains to economic policy and commerce and the court should desist from interfering. Not convinced by this, the bench said, “Should they (pharma companies) be allowed to run amok? What is the justification for the difference in prices? You are not able to come with an answer. We have asked you 30 times. Do not talk about control... You are talking about economic policy and commerce. Is commerce more important than the life of citizens and be given precedence?”Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Californian’s bill targets negligent pet boarding facilities after dog’s viral death
articles.summary: DJ Andrew Fedyk and his wife, Madeleine White Fedyk, posted about their dog, Dunkin, dying at a boarding and training establishment in the state.
articles.body: After an influencer couple went viral in August when their dog died at a boarding facility, a congressman from California has introduced a bill to hold facilities more accountable when pets are harmed or killed. Republican Rep. James Gallagher introduced the legislation, called “Dunkin’s Law,” named for the couple’s Bernese mountain dog. It would expand the state’s Animal Welfare Act “to provide for the protection of companion animals held or cared for at certain facilities,” according to the bill’s text. The bill would classify pets as “sentient beings” and allow owners of pets that were harmed or killed at boarding and similar facilities to bring action against the facilities to recover damages and other lost expenses. “There needs to be greater protections and teeth when something like this happens,” Gallagher told NBC News on Tuesday. He said he hopes not only that the legislation protects families of pets that were hurt or that died but that it also ensures that no-kill shelters do not euthanize dogs and cats in “these horrific ways.” “Make these people actually live up to their word, have accountability, especially for the kind of mistreatment and neglect that we’ve seen in these cases,” Gallagher said. “Hopefully, what it ultimately leads to is this doesn’t happen, that the disincentives are so strong that these guys really up their game and we don’t have bad actors.” Two events prompted Gallagher to introduce the bill, he said in a release accompanying the announcement. The first occurred in June, when Humboldt County sheriff’s investigators uncovered mass burial sites at a Northern California animal rescue facility. As part of an investigation into the shelter, officials recovered intact remains of 117 dogs, as well as other skeletal remains. Preliminary examinations of some of the dogs’ remains showed evidence of gunshot wounds. “What investigators uncovered in Humboldt County is absolutely sickening,” Gallagher said in the release. “People entrusted these animals to a rescue believing they would be protected, only for authorities to discover more than a hundred dead dogs buried on the property.” The second was in August, when Loud Luxury DJ Andrew Fedyk and his wife, Madeleine White Fedyk, said their dog Dunkin died at a board-and-train facility in Los Angeles. Andrew Fedyk told NBC News in September that they chose to leave their two dogs, Dunkin and Poutine, at Smart Dogs Training, which is owned and operated by trainer Jeff Todd, while they went on vacation. He said that they found the business’ page online and that the flood of positive reviews prompted them to book their dogs, thinking basic leash training could help their already well-behaved pets. But hours after they arrived in Europe, Fedyk said, Todd called to tell him Dunkin had died. Todd is alleged to have told Fedyk that the two dogs had been playing outside during a heat wave and that Dunkin died on the way to a separate boarding facility after “showing signs of heat exhaustion.” Fedyk said Todd did not take Dunkin to a veterinarian. Poutine was OK and was later returned to the Fedyks. Fedyk and his wife shared Dunkin’s story with their combined almost 2.5 million followers on social media, which he said prompted “a bunch of people” to reach out with individual stories about similar experiences. Andrew Fedyk did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday. Todd did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday. When NBC News reached out in August, he declined to comment on Dunkin’s case. In August, Los Angeles Animal Services said it was investigating the incident involving Dunkin. The agency did not immediately respond to an emailed request for more information sent Tuesday morning. Los Angeles police declined to provide recent records for 911 calls and police reports relating to Todd’s address, citing an open investigation. The police department did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment sent Tuesday morning. “Their heartbreaking story, along with the horrific discovery of more than 100 dead dogs at a Northern California rescue, exposes a serious gap in how we protect companion animals and hold those responsible for their care accountable,” Gallagher said of the Fedyks in an Instagram post announcing the legislation. Gallagher said Dunkin’s story is why he is introducing this bill, calling it “legislation that would give pet owners a path to seek justice when their animals suffer harm or neglect at covered facilities, while strengthening accountability for unlawful euthanasia at rescues and shelters.” Gallagher told NBC News on Tuesday that Dunkin’s case spurred the legislation, especially after he spoke to Fedyk and Madeleine White Fedyk, who he said expressed frustration and concern that there was no recourse — even though the couple does not fall within his constituency. “Dunkin represents all of these dogs,” Gallagher said. “These have been some of the most horrendous examples, and we want to make sure it doesn’t ever happen again.”

articles.title: Bend, Oregon, shooter previously said he was bullied and told police he was assaulted at home
articles.summary: Police reports describe incidents in recent years in which Griffin John II told police he was punched by a man who had been seeing his mom and hit by his friend’s sister.
articles.body: The 16-year-old boy who killed three children and a teacher, injuring two other people, at a school in Bend, Oregon, was assaulted twice in recent years, once while he was trying to defend his mother, police records show. In one incident, he told his sister he had been bullied at school, according to police, who wrote that he “likely had a cognitive disability.” Griffin John II opened fire on a special-needs classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15 before he was killed by a man who has two daughters at the school. Much about John remains unknown, and law enforcement is still investigating him and any potential motive. But the police reports show he experienced violence at a young age. Court and police records previously obtained by NBC News detailed a tumultuous home life, with both parents being involved in violent encounters and run-ins with law enforcement, as well as financial instability. At age 11, his sister’s friend assaulted him at his home, according to allegations in a Bend police report first obtained by NBC affiliate KGW. John’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told police in the 2022 incident that the friend “slapped John across the face, causing him to chip a tooth,” according to the report. The friend also “punched John in the back of the head,” according to the report. Nickerson told police that John “had special needs,” and the officer wrote that it appeared he had a cognitive disability, given his “non verbal speech communication and speech patterns.” John told the officer that after he came home, his sister’s friend asked him whether he wanted to fight and then slapped him, chipping his tooth, according to the report. The officer noticed a small chip on one of John’s lower front teeth, according to the report. John then said the friend “punched him in the back of the head 4 to 6 times,” it said. John’s sister told the officer that when she got home earlier, John was upset and crying because, he said, he was being bullied at school. “John expressed concerns about reporting the bullying at school because his mom would get upset,” the officer wrote. The officer said that he tried to contact the friend but that all of the numbers associated with the friend were disconnected or no longer in service. Another officer later went to the home and was also unable to speak with the friend, according to the report. A little more than three years later, in 2025, John was punched multiple times by a man Nickerson had a relationship with, according to a Bend police report. The man fled when Nickerson called 911, she told police. Nickerson said she had been arguing with the man about his involvement with other women when she placed all of his belongings outside her apartment. The man then came to the apartment, banged on the front door and eventually forced himself inside, according to the police report. John told police that the man threatened to beat him and his mother up, according to the police report. The domestic dispute turned physical when, John said, he tried to stand up for his mother as the man refused to leave the apartment, Nickerson told police. The man “began to get violent, and I didn’t want him to hurt my mom at all,” John told police. John said that he told the man he needed to leave and that the man shoved him twice, which made him drop his phone. When John went to pick up his phone, the man “bodyslammed” him to the ground, wrapping his arm around his head and neck, according to the report. The man then punched John in the head about 12 to 14 times, John told the officer. The man left after he learned police would be on their way, according to the report. Nickerson and John ultimately decided they did not want to cooperate in an investigation and pursue charges, saying the matter had been resolved, according to the report.

articles.title: Over 100 killed, 113 injured in drone strike on Sudan market
articles.summary: More than 100 people were killed and 113 injured in a drone strike on a crowded market in Nyala, South Darfur, on Monday evening, according to rights
articles.body: More than 100 people were killed and 113 injured in a drone strike on a crowded market in Nyala, South Darfur, on Monday evening, according to rights groups and local officials cited by The Associated Press and Radio Tamazuj.Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence in Sudan, said in a statement on Tuesday that the strike hit Tanqong Market in the Dumaya neighbourhood of Nyala, a city controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The group blamed the Sudanese military for the attack and called for an independent investigation.Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said 36 bodies had arrived at its hospital in Nyala and that its emergency room had treated 150 injured people, AP reported.Dr Alaa al-Din Nugud, health minister in the RSF-aligned Tasis administration, told Radio Tamazuj that 102 civilians were killed and 113 injured. He said a medical team was sent to the scene immediately after the strike and that hospitals and health centres had been placed on alert.Adam Musa Obama, executive director of the Darfur Victims Organization, told Radio Tamazuj that eyewitnesses reported drones associated with the army had struck the market while civilians were shopping and eating breakfast. He said his organisation had documented 14 civilian deaths, including 12 women and six children, while witnesses reported 120 people killed or wounded.AP report cited Emergency Lawyers’ toll of more than 100 killed and 113 injured, while MSF reported receiving 36 bodies and seeing 150 injured at its hospital.Drone strikes have increasingly threatened civilians during Sudan’s war, with both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF using explosive-laden drones. Recent attacks have hit civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, schools, markets and displacement camps. The United Nations has described drone strikes as the deadliest threat to civilians in the conflict.Sudan has been at war since April 2023, when fighting between the SAF and the RSF erupted in Khartoum and spread across the country. The conflict has killed tens of thousands, displaced millions and created what the UN describes as the world’s largest humanitarian crisis, with about 34 million people in need of assistance.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue announced its closure after going viral over its masking policy, with owners citing a lack of leadership for the transition.
articles.body: Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue, a Massachusetts lesbian bar that went viral for its masking policy last month, announced Monday that it would be closing and seeking a buyer for the business. "WE ARE CLOSING. We have put our lives on hold to foster networks of care, resources, and a home base for organizing. It's time we pass it on. We've been fighting since the beginning to fill out the team, and we still don't have a board/leadership to manage workers owned Co-op transfer. We are SOFT CLOSING effective immediately, all BOOKED events will CONTINUE, otherwise we are CLOSED," the bar wrote on Instagram. "We need new owners ASAP, we close this winter," the bar also wrote. Fox News Digital reached out to the bar for comment but did not immediately receive a response. PHILLY GAY SPORTS BAR CANCELED BY ITS OWN FOR NOT BEING GAY ENOUGH ON EVE OF WNBA FINALS Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue went viral last month after The Boston Globe reported that it would be lifting its mask mandate for one night a week. Some critics accused the Massachusetts bar's owners of putting disabled people at risk and compared the policy change to a "mass disabling event" and a "eugenicist" attack while also making threats against the establishment. After The Boston Globe article was published, a Massachusetts chapter of the Communist Party released a statement condemning the piece for being used as a tool to divide the LGBTQ community. "The Western Massachusetts CPUSA rejects the use of conflicts among LGBTQIA+ people and organizations as a tool of division by the extreme right. We reaffirm our solidarity with all those struggling against the genocide of transgender people," the statement read. BOSTON GLOBE OP-ED SAYS VIOLENCE AGAINST TRANSGENDER PEOPLE IS 'GOING DOWN' DESPITE ACTIVIST CLAIMS Fox News host and comedian Jimmy Failla and Fox News contributor Kennedy mocked the story on Failla's "Fox Across America" show last month. "Here's where the free market is beautiful," Kennedy said. "If there's a market for this, and you sell yourselves as safe and mask mandatory and all that stuff and that's when you're making your money, have at it. If that is not working, let the market decide." Failla added, "In a post-Covid world, we placated the biggest moon bats, people we would have otherwise had laughed at and dismissed. And now, unfortunately, this is a big thing on the left that they created. They call these people the heroes, the pioneers and the people worth celebrating. So now, they just show up and air grievances, and they expect to be catered to. But you know who doesn't cater to that? The free market, like you said. And now this business is going under." MAHER BLASTS ‘INTOLERANT LEFT’ AFTER MASSACHUSETTS LESBIAN BAR FACES FURY FOR TWEAKING COVID-ERA MASK POLICY The Boston Globe previously reported that the bar was struggling financially before altering its mask policies. Two of its owners stepped back from daily operations months ago, including one who had enrolled in clown school and another who is a drag performer using it/its pronouns. articles.title: A Michigan home inspection triggered a $150,000 price-cut fight; six years later, an appeals court wiped out a $1.55 million judgment against the buyers
articles.summary: Buying a house was supposed to be a new beginning for a Michigan couple looking for more space for their growing family.
articles.body: Buying a house was supposed to be a new beginning for a Michigan couple looking for more space for their growing family. Roger Lewis and Nicole Susser found a home in Franklin Village and agreed to pay $1.275 million for it in November 2020. But a request to lower the price by $150,000 after an inspection led to a disagreement that lasted nearly six years. The couple never got the house and were eventually ordered to pay more than $1.55 million. On Friday, October 23, the Michigan Court of Appeals overturned that judgment.According to the judgment document available on Justia, the trouble began when the couple raised concerns about the condition of the property. They wanted the seller, Robert Blumberg, to reduce the price. He refused, and even when they lowered their request twice, he did not agree.Lewis and Susser eventually decided they were willing to buy the house for the original price. But by then, Blumberg wanted to cancel the sale. Questions about his former wife's name appearing on the property's ownership records made the situation even more complicated.The disagreement eventually reached court, with both sides blaming each other for the failed purchase. A jury initially ruled in favour of Blumberg, but the appeals court has now found that mistakes during the trial affected the verdict. The case will return to the lower court for further proceedings.How a home inspection changed everythingLewis and Susser signed the purchase agreement on November 22, 2020. The house was being sold in its existing condition, but the agreement allowed them to have it inspected before completing the purchase.The inspection raised what the couple described as major problems. They first asked for $150,000 off the price. When Blumberg refused, they reduced their request to $75,000 and then $35,000. Neither offer worked.According to the court ruling, Blumberg later told the jury that the requests had angered him and made him want to withdraw from the deal.On December 6, he signed paperwork to cancel the purchase and return the buyers' deposit. Lewis and Susser, however, did not sign it. Instead, they told his representatives that they were ready to buy the property without a discount.Why the couple never moved into the houseAnother problem emerged when the property's ownership records were checked. Blumberg's former wife was still named on the title, and he had been advised that this could prevent him from completing the sale under the existing agreement.Blumberg was willing to consider selling at the original price, but wanted to find another home before moving out. He would not promise when he could complete the transaction.Lewis and Susser wanted to stick to the dates already agreed upon. The purchase was supposed to be completed between January 11 and 15, 2021, with the buyers getting possession immediately afterwards.Their lender cleared them to proceed, but the sale never happened. On January 25, 2021, the couple sued Blumberg, asking the court to make him honour the agreement.During the case, it emerged that Blumberg's divorce judgment had already dealt with the ownership issue. His former wife's additional signature was not needed to transfer clear title.One more attempt to sell the house failedEven after the lawsuit began, both sides tried to find a way to complete the sale. They discussed another closing in March 2021, but could not agree on all the conditions.One disagreement involved responsibility for any damage to the property if Blumberg stayed there briefly after the sale.On March 15, Blumberg attended a title company with his former wife and others. Documents to transfer the house were signed, but Lewis and Susser did not attend.The buyers said they had never agreed to complete the purchase under those terms. Blumberg maintained that he was ready to sell and that the couple had failed to go ahead.He later filed claims against them, and the case went to trial. The jury found that Lewis and Susser had broken the purchase agreement, while Blumberg had not.The lower court awarded also Blumberg $1.275 million for the unpaid house price, $255,000 in interest and the couple's $20,000 deposit, along with additional interest and costs. However, the judgment allowed the buyers a credit of up to $1.275 million if Blumberg sold the property to someone else.Why appeals court overturned judgmentLewis and Susser challenged the ruling, and the appeals court found two problems with the way the trial had been conducted.The first concerned the unsuccessful discussions held after the lawsuit began. The judges found that information from those settlement talks had wrongly been used to help decide who was responsible for the failed sale.The second concerned an argument made by the buyers. They said Blumberg had already made it clear, before the January 2021 deadline, that he would not complete the sale under the original terms.The court said the jury should have been told about a legal principle called anticipatory repudiation. Put simply, if someone clearly indicates they will not fulfil a contract before the agreed deadline, the other party may no longer be required to carry out certain obligations.The judges therefore overturned both the ruling against Lewis and Susser and the financial judgment that followed. However, the decision does not mean the couple have finally won the property dispute. The appeals court has not decided which side broke the original agreement. That question remains open as the case returns to the lower court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Suspected shark knocks fisherman off kayak a mile off California coast, forcing swim to shore
articles.summary: A fisherman swam to shore after a suspected shark struck his kayak near Leffingwell Landing in Cambria, puncturing the hull and capsizing it.
articles.body: A California fisherman was forced to swim to shore after a suspected shark struck his kayak about a mile offshore, capsizing the vessel and leaving it too damaged to stay afloat, according to fire officials. The fisherman was near Leffingwell Landing in Cambria around 9:30 a.m. Monday when something struck the underside of his kayak, throwing him into the water, the Cambria Fire Department said in a Facebook post. He managed to climb back aboard and paddle toward shore, but punctures in the hull caused the kayak to fill with water, forcing him to swim the rest of the way. SHARK BITES FISHERMAN TWICE DURING KAYAKING ENCOUNTER ALONG CALIFORNIA BEACH The fisherman reached shore without injuries, according to the department. Firefighters responded after he reached land and launched a rescue boat to recover the damaged kayak, along with his fishing gear and personal belongings. Dr. Chris Lowe of California State University, Long Beach's Shark Lab reviewed photographs of the damage and determined it was reasonable to suspect a shark was responsible, according to the fire department. However, officials emphasized that shark involvement has not been definitively confirmed. CALIFORNIA SCIENTISTS DEVELOPING SHARK-SPOTTING ROBOT AHEAD OF 2028 LOS ANGELES OLYMPICS The area has seen similar encounters before. In May 2012, a shark struck a fishing kayak near Leffingwell Landing, throwing fisherman Joey Nocchi into the water and damaging his vessel. Nocchi escaped without injuries, according to California Department of Fish and Wildlife records and reports from the time. Another fisherman, David Zamora, reported a similar encounter near Cambria in 2019, when a roughly 10-foot great white shark bit his kayak about two miles offshore from Leffingwell Landing, according to local news outlet KSBY. Zamora was thrown into the water but managed to climb back aboard before a nearby boater rescued him. He was not injured. California has documented 233 shark incidents since 1950, including 36 involving kayaking or canoeing, according to Department of Fish and Wildlife figures updated in January 2026. The agency's records include encounters in which sharks make contact with kayaks, surfboards or other equipment, even when no injuries occur. State wildlife officials say some white shark encounters may involve exploratory bites as the animals investigate unfamiliar objects in the water, including kayaks. Such behavior does not necessarily indicate that a shark was attempting to prey on a person. SHARK WEEK PUTS SHARK BITE SURVIVAL IN FOCUS WITH ER DOC'S EXPERT TIPS Following Monday's suspected encounter, the Cambria Fire Department urged ocean users to exercise additional caution, remain aware of their surroundings and avoid entering the water when sharks are visibly active. articles.title: U.S. woman convicted of getting Islamic State training after becoming teen bride to a fighter
articles.summary: Prosecutors said Halima Salman pledged loyalty to the extremist group and willingly participated in its activities. She faces up to 10 years in prison.
articles.body: A New York woman whose father took her to Syria as a teenager and arranged her marriage to an Islamic State fighter was convicted Tuesday of receiving weapons training from the militant group. Prosecutors said Halima Salman, a U.S. citizen, pledged loyalty to the extremist group and willingly participated in its activities. Jurors were shown a video of her holding an assault rifle, a photo of her with the group's flag and loving text messages she sent her husband. Brooklyn-based U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said in a statement that the verdict held Salman “accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization.” The defense sought to portray Salman, now 27, as a teenager who was unwittingly trapped in Syria's civil war, first by her father and later by an extremist husband whose orders she had to follow. “You try to leave, it is death,” Salman testified. She said she refused to be “married off” at age 18 and repeatedly tried to get a divorce. Salman, her mother and even her defense attorneys wept after hearing the verdict. Still in tears, Salman and her mother later hugged each other across the railing between the audience and the courtroom well. Jurors, who began deliberating Thursday, had repeatedly indicated Monday that they were struggling to reach a unanimous decision. The members declined to comment as they left court after the verdict. Salman's lawyers also declined to comment. They are asking the judge to set aside the verdict and acquit her, as federal law allows if a judge finds the evidence presented at a trial doesn't legally support a conviction. Such requests are often made but rarely granted. Salman’s conviction carries the potential for up to 10 years in prison. Sentencing currently is set for Feb. 2. The Islamic State group, which the U.S. government designates as a terrorist group, seized large parts of Iraq and Syria in 2014 and declared the territory to be a caliphate. Despite its defeat in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria two years later, the group still has sleeper cells that carry out deadly attacks in both countries. Born in Brooklyn, Salman was 17 when her father took the family on what she thought was a trip to visit relatives in Turkey in 2017. Instead, the van crossed into Syria, where masked gunmen surrounded them. Salman said she was frightened and confused and had no idea where her father was taking them. “I do blame my father for a lot of things that happened,” she testified. She said she spent three months in housing run by the Islamic State group before reuniting with her family. They moved twice because their homes were hit by airstrikes. On the first day of her marriage, Salman recalled, her husband told her: “Get up, stupid wife, it’s time for you to be a wife.” She spent much of the marriage doing domestic labor for her husband and mother-in-law. Her father died after being injured in an airstrike in 2018. Prosecutors insisted Salman was dishonest and had more agency in Syria than she claimed. They got her to concede during cross-examination that she once sent a religious song about Osama bin Laden to her husband. Prosecutors also disputed Salman’s account of a poor marriage, citing two loving text messages she sent to her husband. “The evidence shows that the defendant received military training from a violent, brutal, terrorist organization — an organization that is responsible for attacks across the world,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda Shami told the jury in a closing argument last week. Salman's husband took a video of her holding an assault rifle, which prosecutors said she had been trained to use. When she testified, Salman said she was only complying with her husband’s request to carry the rifle. She recalled that her last year of marriage was particularly harrowing, as constant bombings sometimes forced them to live in the streets, where she recalled seeing “dead bodies everywhere.” The couple eventually fled with other refugees in a truck, where she told her husband they were going to separate, and Salman testified that she never saw him again. She was detained in Baghouz, Syria, in 2019 by forces opposed to the Islamic State group. She was arrested by U.S. authorities when she returned to New York in 2024.

articles.title: Women's alcohol deaths are increasing - my daughter died alone after fighting for decades
articles.summary: A mum from Aberdeen tells how her daughter died alone after decades fighting alcoholism as records show a rise in female alcohol-related deaths.
articles.body:
The number of women who died last year in Scotland from alcohol-related illnesses was up by 3% on the year before, official figures show.

Overall, the total number of people who died from alcohol-related conditions fell slightly, to the lowest rate since the pandemic. There were 1,152 alcohol-specific deaths registered in Scotland, a decrease of 3% compared with 2024.

The Scottish government said the drop amounted to progress and that it would invest £160m this year on alcohol and drugs programmes.

But one mother from Aberdeen whose daughter died alone after decades fighting alcoholism described her illness as "relentless" and said sometimes all the resources available are still not enough to beat it.

Paula Gibson's daughter Clare died in November 2023, aged 45, after spending the last 20 years of her life in and out of rehab. She had periods of sobriety, but ultimately died at home alone.

The 72-year-old said her daughter started struggling with alcohol in her early-20s but over the next decade her behaviour escalated, even with help and and interventions.

This led to Clare's parents taking custody of her youngest son, Craig, who was eight at the time.

"It probably took about 10 years of feeling like something wasn't quite right, while trying to support her through conversations, but it wasn't enough.

"Her behaviour was extreme and the impact it had on all of us was really difficult.

"We were living on a knife edge, not knowing what the next phone call would be or what would happen to her next.

"Her wellbeing became compromised. She was not making any rational decisions or the right choices for her or her kids," she said.

With both of Clare's sons living with their grandparents, the family tried to maintain their relationship, but it became difficult when the addiction took over, Paula said.

"We were at family centres trying to negotiate any kind of relationship with the boys. We tried to always keep contact between them because you want them to always be a family.

"But she would rock up drunk and we would have to cancel the meetings immediately or I would go to her house to pick her up and she'd fall into the car with a bottle of vodka in her bag.

"It was dreadful and mortifyingly embarrassing and difficult for the boys."

Things escalated months before Clare's death when she went into rehab while her younger son and parents went on a holiday to Greece.

She didn't make it through rehab and during a hospital stay was told that if she did not change her lifestyle she would die.

Paula said the boys had been looking forward to seeing their mother after rehab in a safe setting and breaking the news was one of the hardest moments of her life.

"Clare had been sober leading up to this and phoned me in floods of tears and emotion in a very genuine way.

"We were both weeping on the phone and I told her to go back into rehab and she would get through this.

"I told her I loved her and I would see her when we got back from Greece."

When the family got back, they received a phone call from a painter who was doing work in the house, who had found Clare.

She was not in rehab and had passed out drunk at the bottom of a set of stairs.

"We drove back from Glasgow Airport to Aberdeen and I had to tell them mum had failed rehab and they couldn't see her because she was drunk.

"This was the hardest thing ever because this time we really thought she was on the road to recovery.

"Within two months she was dead," Paula said.

On the night she died, Clare had reached out to emergency services overnight but it was a social worker who found her in the morning.

She died of fatty liver disease, or alcohol-related liver disease (ARLD), where the liver is damaged by drinking too much alcohol over a long period.

Paula spent over 20 years supporting her daughter and said they had all the resources you could need - but sometimes that it is not enough.

She said, despite everything, Clare left a financial legacy so her children would be looked after.

"We spent so many decades living on edge and waiting for that phone call, so that when we found out Clare had died there was a sense of relief - she was finally at peace.

"The alcoholism is a self-fulfilling prophecy and a nasty cycle of horror for those in it and everyone around them.

"She was just like Jekyll and Hyde with a drink, that's the reality and it is hell."

Scottish Health Action on Alcohol Problems said they welcomed the fall in alcohol deaths but raised concern over rising deaths among women.

Charity chairman, Dr Alastair MacGilchrist, said: "It is deeply concerning that while deaths among men have fallen, deaths among women have risen.

"This comes after years in which the alcohol industry has made a targeted effort to encourage more women to drink, from products and packaging designed to appeal to women to marketing that links alcohol with wellbeing, celebration and empowerment."

MacGilchrist also said that alcohol deaths rose sharply during the pandemic and had been slow to come down.

"Despite this year's fall, deaths remain higher than they were before Covid, and people living in Scotland's most deprived areas are now 4.8 times more likely to die from alcohol than those in the least deprived.

"That is not a situation we can accept as the new normal. It is a reason to act," he added.
