articles.title: Emergency supplies advice is not realistic, say low income families
articles.summary: Some families say they cannot afford to stockpile in line with the government's advice.
articles.body:
A single mum has said following government advice to stock up on emergency supplies would mean sacrificing her childcare budget for the school holidays.

Samantha Richards, who works full-time and relies on Universal Credit and her son's disability allowance to cover the bills, said the call to prepare reminded her of the "survival of the fittest".

Last week, Wes Streeting said people should have water , tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.

But one professor said the guidance "will appear at best tone deaf and at worst almost insulting" to households facing poverty.

The UK government said people did not need to buy everything at once.

The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.

But not everyone has the disposable income that allows these types of purchases, said Samantha, 47.

"I think the advice is good, but we do want to know what [the government] plan to do in the event of us needing this.

Samantha takes part in Changing Realities, a collaboration between more than 200 parents and carers on a low income from across the UK.

She has torches and blankets already and never lets food in the house completely run out.

But her autistic son's safe foods require a fridge and freezer, and she worries if an emergency did happen, he would not be able to eat the tinned food if she did buy it.

Instead, they would need to rely on other items in the cupboard.

"You may not feel very well after a few days but you can last more than three without eating," Samantha said.

But you can't last very long without water, she believes, so that is what she will prioritise.

According to University of Glasgow professor Ruth Patrick, the UK government's guidance "will appear at best tone deaf and at worst almost insulting to the 14 million households currently facing poverty across the UK".

She is leading the Changing Realities project, and added: "There is a profound mis-match between this suggestion and the daily realities for parents and carers on a low-income up and down the country who are struggling to get by, especially as costs continue to rise and the temperatures drop."

"Preparedness shouldn't be just for people that really truly can afford to," said Ana, founder of UK Preppers Club on Facebook.

She said she was disappointed in the UK government announcement because it did not give people an idea of what to actually do in an emergency.

Ana said she would have welcomed advice being distributed about what to do if there is no running water - how do you flush your toilet for example?

The 42-year-old from Swansea said she was brought up to have "a rotating pantry" to give herself a safeguard for emergencies, including growing her own food and preserving it.

She said it was Covid which caused her to "up the ante" as she was heavily pregnant and ended up having an emergency C-section.

Unable to naturally feed her baby, she found she did not have enough formula and was quoted £300 online for it, with the supermarkets she tried out of stock.

That was when she started pushing for "preparedness", and said: "Look after your family, then, if something like this happens, you don't have to leave people, like myself at the time, vulnerable."

Ana said even just having a plan of who would pick up your child from school if the power went out, or where the family would meet if their property was inaccessible would be a good start.

"It doesn't have to be the Armageddon's happening, but just generally having a coherent plan of the family. What happens if?" she added.

"What happens if there's no power? What do you do? All those kind of little plans."

Ana said her advice would be for people to pick up an extra tin or pack of crackers every time they shop to slowly build up the supply.

Donna Lloyd, 60, a supply teacher in Denbighshire, has been preparing with her wife since a power cut in the Covid lockdown highlighted that they did not have any way to cook.

She says "in all honesty, no, it is not realistic" for everyone to be able to afford to buy emergency supplies.

Donna believes the UK government should use television programmes to explain how to prepare.

Alongside stockpiling, she also thinks people should learn first aid, how to gather, filter and purify water, and how to power items such as radios and fridges using solar power or power banks or a generator.

Yasmin Ibison, a senior policy adviser at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF) said preparing for emergencies was sensible.

There are 7.4 million low income families in the UK who were unable to afford essential items in the last six months and 1.5 million households across the UK who have used a food bank in the past six months, according to JRF’s cost of living tracker published in July 2026 .

Yasmin added: "When we have millions of people who already can't afford essentials like food, heating, basic toiletries, the question I ask is how are they going to afford to buy additional items in their cupboards if they're already struggling to meet these most basic and everyday needs?"

The UK government said: "This campaign is about providing the public with simple steps to ensure households are properly prepared, freeing up front line services to support those most in need in the case of emergencies like extreme weather or power outages.

"The advice is clear, you don't need to do it all at once. Build up your readiness gradually over time by taking it step by step, and picking up an extra item or two when you can."

articles.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
articles.summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
articles.body:
Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.

Official data released in the last week show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.

The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.

The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.

China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children .

The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.

At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.

The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.

"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.

The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.

China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy , which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.

The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.

The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.

But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.

Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.

Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.

Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.

The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.

The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.

Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.

It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

articles.title: They bought cabins to live on a luxury cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia.
articles.summary: Florida-based Villa Vie Residences said it was working to identify “temporary living arrangements” for people aboard The Odyssey, a 642-foot cruise ship.
articles.body: A residential cruise ship halted operations in Cambodia on Tuesday amid soaring fuel costs, leaving passengers in limbo after the U.S. company that operates it ordered them to disembark. Florida-based Villa Vie Residences said in a news release that it was working to identify “temporary living arrangements” for people aboard The Odyssey, a 642-foot cruise ship that launched from Belfast, Northern Ireland, three years ago and promised passengers “an unparalleled lifestyle of luxury and exploration” as it toured the planet. Cabins on The Odyssey were for sale or rent. According to the company, the ship can accommodate 650 residents; it isn’t clear how many were on board Tuesday or where in Cambodia they disembarked. An executive with the company, Mikael Petterson, declined to provide additional details in an email to NBC News. In a release this year announcing the company’s second residential cruise ship, Petterson said The Odyssey was 85% sold. The company said in Tuesday’s release that it had taken significant measures to reduce fuel consumption but that those steps had failed to offset the spike in costs. Global oil prices have surged since the war with Iran began this year, disrupting the world’s flow of fuel. Oil prices climbed to their highest levels since this spring this month. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” the company said. “Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured.” Randy Cassingham, a resident on the boat, wrote in a blog post that he learned his journey was over after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship shortly after 7 a.m. Monday. The Odyssey was entering a “temporary lay up” period — indicating it would no longer be used — and everyone had to disembark by 2 p.m., the message said, according to Cassingham, who runs ResidentialCruising.com and didn’t immediately reply to an interview request. Cassingham attributed the development to a “cascade of problems” that he would detail later. Pamela Reckamp, who rented a cabin with her husband and disembarked this month, said in an interview that she wasn’t surprised that the ship’s journey was over. Reckamp, 59, recalled having attended a meeting in early September at which a company official asked cabin owners to help them raise $1 million so they could leave Ha Long Bay, Vietnam. “She said, ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp recalled. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’” When the ship’s financial issues were raised during another meeting a few weeks later, Reckamp recalled, a woman stood up and said she’d bought a cabin in August and hadn’t been made aware of the issues. “I sold my house,” Reckamp recalled the woman saying. “I sold my car. I bought my home on this ship.” Reckamp said she felt terrible for the residents and the staff, who she said were lovely. “We dodged a bullet,” she added. Villa Vie Residences didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday night. In a lawsuit filed last year, a company that bought a cabin on The Odyssey for $469,000 accused Villa Vie Residences of fraud, alleging it misrepresented its financial stability. The company’s business model was not financially sound, the suit alleges, “but rather precarious.” The plaintiffs are asking for a jury trial and unspecified damages of more than $100,000. Villa Vie Residences denied the allegations in the suit, which is ongoing. Other cabins on the ship were available for significantly less money. Even though 85% of the ship was sold, the company said in 2024, prospective residents could still “secure their dream home starting at just $119,000.” “When we launched Odyssey, we set out to prove that residential cruising wasn’t just possible — it was sustainable,” Petterson said in July.

articles.title: MS patient left in 'horrific' pain amid UK wide medicine shortage
articles.summary: Jill Kenning says she has been unable to get a drug she uses to manage her condition.
articles.body:
A woman with multiple sclerosis (MS) has said she is living with "horrific pain" after being unable to get a drug she uses to manage her condition.

Jill Kenning has used Nabilone for 17 of the 18 years since she was diagnosed with MS and said the drug had been vital for managing her pain and helping her live a normal life.

She said she had spent most of her time in bed since running out of the drug last Tuesday.

Northern Ireland's devolved health department said there was disruption to supplies of the drug across the UK, meaning Nabilone was out of stock with wholesalers and not expected to be available again until December.

A spokesperson said they would not say why there was disruption as the information was "commercially sensitive".

According to a tracker published by the industry reference guide MIMS, the average number of drugs in short supply in the UK has trended upward this year .

The number of drugs in short supply reached 157 this week, up from a low of 107 in January.

Pharmacists warn of medicine shortages in NI

The struggle to get hold of medication in England is set to get worse

'Life-changing' MS drug to help people walk now on NHS in England

Kenning, from Coleraine in County Londonderry, was diagnosed with MS in 2008 after experiencing problems with her sight.

She subsequently developed numbness down the left side of her body and was treated by a neurologist.

After a severe relapse, which resulted in a four-week hospital stay, she was prescribed Nabilone which she said made a massive difference to her quality of life.

"It helps me basically that I can get out of bed in the morning," she said.

But she said that without the drug she experienced constant pain in her eye, which she compared to being "stabbed with a hot poker".

After contacting her health trust for her regular repeat prescription, she said she was told there were no supplies of Nabilone available.

She was told to contact her neurologist and has since been prescribed other medication.

Kenning said the alternatives had not been effective and that her health had declined to the point where she had to stay in hospital for several nights.

"I don't want to be here any more because the pain is so bad," she said.

"I have been living on painkillers... I can't sleep, I'm sick, I'm not eating."

Kenning said more should have been done to prepare patients for the disruption.

"How do I live my life? How do I cope with the pain?" she said.

"I'm not only fighting for me, I'm fighting for all the other patients that are on this drug."

Multiple sclerosis is a disease that affects nerves in the brain and spinal cord.

The nerves in these areas are surrounded by a protein called myelin, which helps signals from the brain get to the rest of the body.

The myelin becomes damaged in people with MS because the immune system mistakes it for something that shouldn't be there and attacks it.

This means signals from the brain struggle to get through properly.

Northern Ireland's Department of Health (DoH) said both licensed doses of Nabilone were out of stock from wholesalers across the UK.

It said the shortage began affecting 1mg capsules in July, with the 0.25mg strength becoming unavailable more recently.

The DoH said it was working with the UK's Department of Health and Social Care and health trusts to manage the disruption, and that guidance had been issued to healthcare professionals on alternative treatments, including unlicensed imports of Nabilone where available.

A spokesperson said the DoH recognised "that medicine supply disruptions can be concerning for patients and the healthcare professionals who care for them".

"If patients cannot access their prescribed medication or have concerns about an alternative, they should speak to their specialist healthcare teams for advice about their treatment options," the spokesperson said.

articles.title: Drone technology: Start-ups look for ways to make quieter drones
articles.summary: As drone deliveries become more commonplace, their makers are looking for ways to make them quieter.
articles.body:
Nature lover Ashley Schmidt no longer spends much time in her garden, in the Dallas suburb of North Garland.

She's also given up on cycling to the local parks where she previously enjoyed taking close-up photos of the bugs, lizards and toads.

It's all because she can't stand the sound of the delivery drones that fly overhead, depositing her neighbours' online orders.

"They emit this very annoying buzz. It triggers my fight or flight response," says the 44-year-old administrative assistant.

"You can hear the drones on approach and you can hear them inside your home when they pass directly overhead and then you hear them as they leave," she says.

Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.

Delivery drone services, not long ago a novelty, are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US.

Among them, Amazon Prime Air is in the process of expanding deliveries to nearly 500 cities and towns, delivering items that fit into a space the size of a shoe box. It has also launched to customers in and around Darlington in the north of England.

Smaller drone delivery services are popping up too: in some US cities, customers can order flying treats from their local pizza joint or ice cream parlour.

Even in cities where noise is already a steady part of life, the sound of drones seems to irk in a particular way.

While the steady passing of traffic might blend into the background, the sudden whine of a drone's rotors can pierce the everyday hum.

The sound tends to be "particularly noticeable, even when overall sound levels are relatively low," says Antonio Torija Martinez, professor in acoustic engineering and psychoacoustics at the University of Salford.

Unlike planes, drones operate at low altitudes and may fly directly over residential areas.

"They can expose communities that have not previously experienced significant aircraft noise, and who may therefore be more sensitive to changes in their local soundscape," says Torija Martinez.

He points to research showing that people respond strongly to a noise when they consider the source to be "novel, intrusive or frequent". People who benefit from a drone delivery service, for example, may be less bothered by the noise.

However, complaints about the sound of drones are likely to grow, he warns: "At the moment we are seeing some of these problems localised in some areas, but… as the drone sector expands, more and more of these complaints will happen."

In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates commercial drones, but it has come under fire for allowing noisy drone delivery operations. The FAA says operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for addressing any community concerns.

Might better technology muffle the irritating buzz?

One startup, Greenjets, set out to tackle both "noise level and the frequency of that noise," as Darren James, future technologies lead at the company, puts it.

The London-based business has designed a propulsion system it claims can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds.

While standard drones use spinning propellers that slice through open air, creating that high-pitched buzz, Greenjets encloses spinning blades inside a pod, to muffle the sound and direct the noise away from the ground.

Its system also quietens things down through slower rotor speed and by using materials that reduce vibration noise.

Making quieter drones isn't just about keeping the noise down for neighbours who are already sick of airborne deliveries.

Greenjets' low-noise tech has been used by police and harbour security teams in Germany. It has also helped conservationists in Africa, who are seeking to track poachers from above without being detected.

Battlefield drone operators also have good reason to keep the noise down, to avoid alerting the enemy of the approach of their unmanned vehicles.

"There are some efforts to reduce the sound of drones. The US Special Forces are interested, at an experimental stage," says Robert Tollast, a research fellow at Whitehall think tank The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

But he stresses that drone speed, rather than stealthiness, tends to come first for larger drones used in the war between Russia and Ukraine. "Make it faster, not less quiet, seems to be the approach," says Tollast.

For Detroit-based entrepreneur, Greg Sharrow, it was the challenge of broadcasting a classical music performance back in 2012 that set him on the path to quieter drone design.

He needed to film a violinist from a tricky angle and a drone seemed the only solution – expect that it would be far too noisy.

As a starting point, "I knew that most of the noise from the drone was coming from the propeller, not the motor," he says. Specifically, it was the tips of the blades that he realised were creating the noise as they swiped through the air.

"I asked myself a very simple question, what would a tipless propeller look like and how would it function?"

The result was to create a propeller with twisted loop-shaped blades with no points.

It turned out it was easier to test his propeller in water than it was to repeatedly fly a drone, which led Sharrow to initially develop a less noisy boat propeller. Now, however, his company, Sharrow Engineering, is focusing on developing "ultra-quiet" drone rotors.

"We have validated that the technology works in drone applications and that it is dramatically quieter," says Sharrow.

Companies at the forefront of drone deliveries say they are also working to reduce the noise of their fleets. A spokesperson for Amazon says it has made "measurable sound improvements" to its drones and its latest designs use custom-designed propellers "that produce almost half the perceived sound of the prior generation, with a milder tone".

Drone maker Wing, which provides its vehicles for Walmart deliveries, says its propellers are designed to minimise noise. It also varies its flight paths to prevent repeated overflights over any single home or neighbourhood.

For Schmidt, fed up with the noise of drones, the only truly satisfactory solution would be to halt drone deliveries in her area. "I would like them to completely stop until they figure out how their services stop being a nuisance," she says.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Frida Kahlo: "I am my own muse; I am the subject I know best. The subject I want to know better."
articles.summary: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter who is popularly known even today for creating astonishing self-portraits.
articles.body: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter who is popularly known even today for creating astonishing self-portraits. Her life began and ended in Mexico City, in her home known as the Blue House, as she had polio as a child and lived with injuries from a terrible road accident. She began painting while recovering, and most of her famous works are portraits of herself.But beyond just being a painter, she also spoke many words of wisdom that continue to resurface as valuable ideas today.She once spoke about a profound idea, explaining that most of us spend our days looking outward and notice what others wear, what they post, what they achieve, and somewhere in that noise we forget to look at the one person we spend every single moment with, do we really know ourselves?Let us read further to know what she exactly meansQuote of the dayI am my own muse, I am the subject I know best. The subject I want to know betterWhat does the quote meanTraditionally, a muse is someone who is a lover, a friend, or a mysterious figure who sparks an artist's work, but in the quote famously attributed to Kahlo, according to Good Quotes, she turns this idea around.Inspiration, she suggests, does not have to arrive from outside; it can begin with you. As she explains, nobody else has lived inside your head, felt your fears, or remembered your childhood the way you have, and that could be the driving force behind your work. You are the one subject you have studied every single day of your life.The final line is the most interesting part. Wanting to know the subject better admits that self-knowledge does not have limits, and there is no specific age for learning. Even the person you know best can still surprise you.Her own life shows why this mattered: after her accident, she spent months in plaster body casts and began painting herself with the help of a mirror. She also worked so much on self-portraits because she was so often alone.How are these words relevant today?We are surrounded by images of ourselves today, be it selfies, profiles, stories, and reels that fill our phones. Yet looking at yourself is not the same as knowing yourself. Kahlo reminds us to go deeper and ask why we feel what we feel, what we want, and what we keep avoiding.Even today, this spirit can be seen in the growing popularity of journaling, therapy, and honest storytelling by creators who use their own lives as material. It also carries a lesson in self-dependence and realising that you do not need to wait for approval or a perfect source of inspiration.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Michael J. Fox’s foundation launched a Parkinson’s study in 2010; 16 years later, its data has been downloaded over 50 million times and is helping researchers design more targeted clinical trials
articles.summary: When the Michael J.
articles.body: When the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research launched a major study in 2010, the objective was to help scientists better understand the disease and identify markers that could improve the process of diagnosis and subsequent treatment. Sixteen years later, the initiative has grown into a global research resource. With its data downloaded over 50 million times, it has transformed the nature of Parkinson’s research and drug development.The study, originally known as the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), reached this milestone as researchers began exploring new ways to understand the biological differences between people living with Parkinson’s disease. In May 2026, the foundation announced that the initiative would be renamed the Parkinson’s Precision Medicine Initiative, reflecting the progress made since its launch and a growing focus on treatments tailored to individual patients.The research that grew into a global resourceFor Michael J. Fox, who has publicly shared his experience of living with Parkinson’s disease since disclosing his diagnosis in 1998, the foundation's work has remained focused on advancing research and bettering options for people affected by the condition.Parkinson’s disease is a neurological condition that affects movement, can also cause a range of non-motor symptoms and worsens progressively over time. The foundation has described Parkinson's as “one of the fastest growing neurological diseases in the world.” The report Economic Burden of Parkinson’s and Atypical Parkinsonism in the United States, prepared for the Michael J. Fox Foundation, indicates that the disease affects an estimated 1.2 million Americans and costs the US federal government over $82 billion yearly.While existing treatments can help alleviate certain symptoms, the major global endeavour behind Parkinson's research has been finding ways to relieve the disease's effects. The foundation established PPMI to carry out research on biomarkers, which are measurable biological indicators that can help scientists identify and track a disease. By studying people with Parkinson’s, individuals considered at risk and control participants, researchers could collect information about how the condition develops and changes over time.Over the years, the initiative has expanded beyond its original scope. According to the foundation's May 2026 announcement, it now includes over 4,200 participants attending clinics across 50 sites in 12 countries, alongside more than 47,000 online participants contributing information through its digital platform.The resulting collection of data, biological samples and research findings has become an important resource for scientists investigating Parkinson’s. Rather than each research team having to build its own study from the beginning, investigators worldwide can access PPMI data and use it to explore questions about the disease.Why is the study moving towards precision medicineOne of the most significant developments in Parkinson’s research is the growing understanding that the condition does not necessarily follow the same biological course in every person. The renamed Parkinson’s Precision Medicine Initiative reflects an effort to address this challenge. Precision medicine focuses on understanding the biological characteristics of individual patients rather than treating everyone as though they have precisely the same form of a disease. The foundation has highlighted how PPMI data can help researchers identify disease-related changes earlier, making it easier to develop more sensitive ways to measure changes during clinical trials.These findings could help investigators select participants whose biological characteristics make them more suitable for testing a particular treatment. They could also help researchers determine whether a potential therapy is having the intended effect.MJFF Chief Scientist Mark Frasier, PhD noted that “It’s a tremendously exciting time in Parkinson’s research,” and it certainly is. Some recent and noteworthy breakthroughs involve research using the alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay, which can detect Parkinson’s related biological activity in samples. Work using PPMI samples has helped further this approach, including the possibility of identifying disease related biology even before symptoms appear.While the data and scientific developments have attracted attention, the initiative also depends on the people who contribute their time, health information and biological samples.Thousands of participants have helped build the resource over the past 16 years, allowing researchers to examine the disease across different populations and stages of progression. Their contributions have made it possible to develop a dataset that individual laboratories would find difficult to assemble independently.The foundation has also expanded opportunities for people to participate remotely through its digital research hub , my PPMI. This allows individuals to contribute health information and take part in research without every aspect of their involvement requiring an in-person visit.The initiative's international reach also means that its findings can inform research beyond the institutions where the original information was collected. By making its research and data available, the foundation is helping lay the groundwork for precision medicine in Parkinson research.What comes next for Parkinson’s research?The foundation's next challenge is to turn the knowledge gathered through years of research into more effective ways of identifying, studying and treating Parkinson’s disease.Its data is helping researchers redefine clinical trial designs, investigate differences between patient groups and explore whether potential treatments could be better matched to the people most likely to benefit. Such work remains profound and fundamental in medical research because identifying a promising therapy is only one part of the overall process, but it is a crucial starting point for the research.You use AI every day. articles.title: Man accused of threatening to hijack United flight says it was a drunken joke
articles.summary: Cockpit audio captured a pilot explaining the diverted United Airlines flight while Dante Milne allegedly slept, unaware he caused the emergency.
articles.body: A New Jersey man accused of sending a text threatening to hijack a United Airlines flight over the weekend told investigators he had been drinking and described the message as poorly worded banter with a coworker, according to an arrest report. Dante Milne, 25, allegedly sent the threatening message Saturday while aboard United Airlines Flight 1681, a Boeing 737 carrying 150 passengers and six crew members from Las Vegas to Newark, New Jersey. "I’m gonna hijack this b---- and crash ur row only," Milne allegedly wrote, according to an arrest report cited by FOX5 Vegas. AIRPORT SUSPECT PACKED EXPLOSIVE DEVICE FOR FLIGHT, CAUGHT WITH CRYPTIC MESSAGE ON PHONE: FEDS The message was allegedly spotted by a flight attendant shortly after departure, and the crew alerted the captain, who secured the cockpit and diverted the aircraft back to Harry Reid International Airport, where it landed at approximately 11:05 p.m. The flight was delayed overnight after the crew reached its permitted working hours and departed for Newark the following morning, United Airlines previously told Fox News Digital. Authorities later charged Milne with one count of making threats or conveying false information concerning an act of terrorism. According to an arrest report, Milne told investigators he had consumed a beer and several shots at an airport bar before boarding. FAA EMPLOYEE CHARGED WITH ALLEGEDLY THREATENING TO KILL PRESIDENT TRUMP IN EMAIL TO WHITE HOUSE He said he then fell asleep aboard the plane and woke up to discover the aircraft was returning to Las Vegas. Milne initially acknowledged texting someone aboard the flight but said he could not remember the messages. When investigators specifically asked about the alleged hijacking threat, he described it as poorly worded "banter between coworkers," according to the arrest report. Milne reportedly said he never intended to take control of the aircraft and apologized for what happened. He told detectives he was returning home after spending three days in Las Vegas for an apprenticeship training program involving underwater welding, according to the report. Air traffic control audio previously obtained by ATC.com and reported by Fox News captured the pilot explaining the situation as the flight returned to Las Vegas, including that the passenger suspected of making the threat apparently did not realize the aircraft had turned around because of him. FRONTIER PASSENGERS TACKLE MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY CHOKED OFF-DUTY FLIGHT ATTENDANT, TRIED TO OPEN DOOR MID-FLIGHT "The passenger does not know anything is going on," the pilot told air traffic controllers. "The flight attendant saw him texting that he was going to hijack the aircraft and called me and we went lockdown. … No restraint, passenger is compliant because he’s unaware." Milne was later released on $10,000 bail, and his attorney told a judge Tuesday that he intended to plead not guilty, according to KLAS-TV. Milne is due back in court on Jan. 5. After the incident, United Airlines said the flight had returned to Las Vegas to address a "potential security concern." "United Flight 1681 from Las Vegas to Newark on Saturday, Oct. 24, safely returned to Las Vegas to address a potential security concern," United Airlines previously told Fox News Digital. "The flight was delayed overnight due to crew timeout, and departed for Newark this morning." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) also confirmed that the flight's crew reported a "passenger disturbance" and that the incident remained under investigation. Fox News Digital's Jessica Mekles and Sophia Compton contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘Maxxing’ becomes Dictionary.com’s 2026 Word of the Year: What the viral term means and why it earned the spot
articles.summary: The internet has found a word for its seemingly endless desire to do more, look better, work harder, and optimize almost every aspect of life.
articles.body: The internet has found a word for its seemingly endless desire to do more, look better, work harder, and optimize almost every aspect of life. Enter “maxxing”: the word that captures our restless urge to push ourselves, whether it’s chasing higher productivity at work, obsessing over fitness or appearance, or trying to upgrade even how we sleep. It describes a kind of relentless efficiency that’s become almost a way of life online.Dictionary.com didn’t just stumble on a fun bit of internet slang when they picked “maxxing” as the 2026 Word of the Year on October 26; they grabbed onto a word that seems glued to modern ambition and self-improvement, all while digital life raises the stakes.‘Maxxing’: What does the word even mean?To be honest, “maxxing” didn’t pop up overnight. The buzz started in niche corners of the internet: places where you’d see people talking about “looksmaxxing” (pouring effort into every angle of appearance), “sleepmaxxing” (getting seriously strategic about rest), or “proteinmaxxing” (trying to hit those daily protein goals with scientific precision). The word is sticky, easily snapping onto new contexts, from earnest life upgrades to tongue-in-cheek mockery of just how far we’ll go to optimize... well, anything.That’s the special appeal of the word: you can use “maxxing” to talk about a new workout craze, your latest reading sprint, or even a night spent making your living room extra cozy (“cozymaxxing,” which somehow sounds both silly and inviting). Some people say it straight, others with a smirk. Either way, it reflects this constant internet-fueled pressure to work on ourselves, and the running joke that maybe we’ve all taken the optimization thing a bit too far.But there’s a flip side. The more a word like “maxxing” seeps into daily talk, the clearer it becomes: there’s a kind of tension at the heart of all this. Technology and hyper-connected culture tell us that everything, from work and health to even our downtime, can be hacked, measured, and squeezed for more value. That’d be fine if it always felt empowering. But often, it just feels like the ordinary parts of life have turned into a contest you can win or lose. Sleep isn’t just sleeping; it’s “sleep hygiene” and “tracking REM cycles.” Movie night can end up feeling like a performance, one more thing to “cozymaxx” correctly.That’s probably why “maxxing” stands out. The word is both an invitation and a warning: you can chase the best version of yourself or, if you’re not careful, get caught in a cycle where satisfaction is always just out of reach. There’s a certain honesty to using “maxxing” ironically, poking fun at the urge to optimize even the fun stuff, and maybe, in that joke, a gentle reminder to chill out.Where did the word ‘maxxing’ come from?As for its roots, “maxxing” comes from an old family of words like “maximum” and “maximize.” In gaming circles, “min-maxing” (a strategy of boosting strengths and compensating for weaknesses in a character) crept into wider internet language. The shift to “maxxing,” with that extra “x,” happened over years of meme-ing and forum chatter. By now, you see it everywhere, and not just attached to specific habits. In fact, people talk about “maxxing” their lives in general, as if the entire day’s agenda is a spreadsheet waiting to be optimized.Dictionary.com says their choice always reflects more than raw popularity. They weigh how a word seeps through news stories, online debates, and social media trends. The pick of “maxxing” for 2026 came out of that blur: juggling anxieties about the cost of living, new tech, and the never-ending search for self-betterment, but also the playful and sometimes cynical undertones in the way we talk about it.Why is ‘maxxing’ the Word of the Year for 2026, and who were the other contenders?Of course, “maxxing” wasn’t the only contender for Word of the Year. The shortlist also included words like “affordability” (not exactly a fun topic for anyone struggling with rent or groceries right now), “data center” (a sign of how AI has wormed its way into everything), “odyssey” (fresh off pop culture’s obsession with epic journeys, thanks to a big-budget movie adaptation of Homer), and “unc” (youth slang that lands awkwardly on the ears of, well, uncles everywhere). Each speaks to a different anxiety or fascination of the time.But “maxxing” has that rare knack for linking otherwise scattered trends into a single, energetic and slightly exhausting idea.In the end, the word of the year says a lot about where we are in 2026: always looking for an edge, keeping score, making dinner or downtime feel like a project. Whether people use the word to motivate themselves or just to laugh at how intense things have gotten, “maxxing” holds up a mirror to a world that’s never really off-duty.The real question it raises?
